qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture seventeen. Spiking neural networks, which talk in brief spikes and stay quiet when nothing happens.
Meet Pip, a tiny garden rover on one coin battery.
Pip patrols a garden on one coin battery.
A conventional network updates every neuron on every step, so the battery drains fast.
A conventional ANN computes every neuron, every step.
Pip needs quick reactions, low power, and learning on the go.
Pip needs quick reactions, low power and learning on the go.
A spiking network stays quiet. When a whisker touches a leaf, one neuron spikes, and Pip stops.
An SNN sends discrete spikes only when needed.
Each sensor sends a spike train, and one neuron answers with a train of its own.
A neuron's run of spikes over time is a spike train.
In rate coding, a stronger signal sends more spikes.
Rate coding: a stronger signal sends more spikes.
Dim light gives two spikes in twenty steps, medium five, and bright nine.
Dim 2, medium 5, bright 9 spikes in 20 steps.
Every spike is the same size. Only how many there are carries the message.
Only how many count, not their size.
In temporal coding, a strong input fires early and a weak one late.
Temporal coding: a strong input fires early, a weak one late.
Bright fires at step four, dim at step sixteen. One well-timed spike can be enough.
Bright fires at step 4, dim at step 16. One spike can be enough.
In population coding, five neurons each prefer a range of strengths.
Population coding: five neurons, each liking a range.
A strength of seven wakes the neurons that like five, seven and a half, and ten.
Strength 7 wakes the neurons that like 5, 7.5 and 10.
Charge builds up like drops in a bucket. Eight drops of nought point one two reach nought point nine six, just short of the line.
Charge accumulates from inputs, like drops in a bucket.
With drops of a quarter, it hits the threshold every fourth step, fires, resets and fills again. Five spikes.
At the threshold it fires a spike, resets, and fills again.
Now drill a hole. Charge below the threshold leaks away.
Below-threshold charge leaks away over time.
With drops of nought point two, the level settles near two thirds and never fires.
With this leak the charge levels off near 0.67: no spike.
Spikes spread like ripples. At step one, input A fires.
t = 1: input A fires.
One step later, both of A's neighbours fire.
t = 2: one step later, both of A's neighbours fire.
Neuron O needs three spikes at once. At step three it gets only two.
O needs 3 spikes at once. Two is not enough.
At step four, all four middle neurons fire together.
t = 4: A's and B's neighbours fire together.
So at step five, O receives four spikes, crosses its threshold and fires.
t = 5: O gets 4 spikes, crosses its threshold and fires.
A synapse links a sender, the pre-synaptic neuron, to a receiver, the post-synaptic neuron.
A synapse links a pre-synaptic sender to a post-synaptic receiver.
When pre fires just before post, the link grows by one each time. That is potentiation.
Pre fires just before post: strengthen. Potentiation.
When post fires first, the link weakens. That is depression.
Post fires before pre: weaken. Depression.
No right answers are needed, only spike timing. That is unsupervised learning.
No labels needed: STDP is unsupervised learning.
Backpropagation works back from the error, using the slope of each neuron.
Backpropagation walks back from the error, using each neuron's slope.
A spiking neuron outputs nought below its threshold, then jumps.
A spiking neuron is 0 below the threshold, then jumps.
Its slope is the Dirac delta, zero everywhere except one thin spike.
Its slope is the Dirac delta: zero everywhere but one point.
The ground is flat everywhere, so plain backpropagation has no gradient to follow.
No gradient information, so plain backprop can't be used.
The fix: real spikes go forward, but the backward pass pretends the neuron is a smooth sigmoid.
Keep real spikes forward; pretend a smooth sigmoid backward.
Its slope is a bell on the threshold. With k of one, the peak is nought point two five.
Its slope is a bell centred on the threshold. k = 1: peak 0.25.
With k of five, the peak is one point two five, and the bell is narrower.
k = 5: peak 1.25, narrower.
With k of twenty, the peak is five. As k grows, the bell becomes the delta.
k = 20: peak 5. As k grows, the bell becomes the delta.
An evolutionary algorithm can tune weights, delays, thresholds, and even the structure.
An EA can tune weights, delays, thresholds and structure.
It is often bi-level: structure on the upper level, weights on the lower one.
Often bi-level: structure upper, weights lower.
Thirty networks a generation for a hundred generations is three thousand tests.
30 networks a generation, 100 generations: 3000 tests.
That is costly, and evolving everything together is still an open challenge.
Costly, and co-evolving everything at once is still open.
Spikes carry information by rate, timing, or which neurons fire.
A leaky neuron fills, fires at its threshold and resets.
They learn by spike order, surrogate slopes, or evolution.
